title: What is Git and how does version control work?
seoTitle: What Is Git? Version Control, Commits and Branches Explained
seoDescription: Learn how Git tracks code history, what commits and branches are, how merging works and how Git differs from GitHub.
excerpt: Git gives software teams a distributed history of changes and a safe way to develop multiple ideas in parallel.
author: KitsuWire Editorial
keyTakeaways: Git is a distributed version-control system that records snapshots of a project's history.
Commits create history, branches provide movable lines of development, and merges combine changes.
Git and GitHub are different: Git is the version-control technology; GitHub is a collaboration and hosting platform built around Git repositories.
body: Software changes constantly. Without version control, developers would be left copying folders, overwriting each other's work and manually remembering which version was deployed. Git gives those changes a structured history.
Git is distributed, meaning a normal clone contains repository history rather than being only a thin connection to one central server.

sections.heading: Repositories, working trees and commits
paragraphs: A Git repository stores project history and metadata. Developers edit files in a working tree, select changes for the staging area and create commits that record a snapshot plus metadata such as author and parent history.
Commits are identified by cryptographic hashes. This makes history content-addressed and allows Git to detect when recorded objects differ.

sections.heading: Why the staging area exists
paragraphs: The staging area lets a developer choose exactly which changes belong in the next commit. A working directory can contain several unfinished edits while the next commit contains only one coherent change.
Small, focused commits make reviews and debugging easier because history communicates intent rather than simply recording everything that happened at once.

sections.heading: Branches and merging
paragraphs: A Git branch is essentially a movable reference to a commit. Creating a branch is cheap, so teams use branches for features, fixes and experiments.

When work is ready, histories can be combined through a merge or reorganized through rebasing. Conflicts occur when Git cannot safely determine how competing changes should be combined and a human must resolve them.

sections.heading: Local and remote repositories
paragraphs: Git works locally, but teams usually synchronize repositories through remotes. Commands such as fetch retrieve remote history, pull integrates changes, and push publishes local commits to a remote repository.
Platforms such as GitHub add pull requests, code review, issue tracking, permissions and CI/CD integrations around this Git workflow.

sections.heading: A healthy Git workflow
paragraphs: Good Git usage is less about memorizing commands and more about creating understandable history. Teams benefit from descriptive commit messages, protected main branches, code review and automated tests.
Secrets, generated artifacts and large binary files should not be committed casually. A .gitignore file helps exclude local or generated content that does not belong in source history.

faq.question: Is Git the same as GitHub?
faq.answer: No. Git is the distributed version-control system. GitHub hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration, automation and project-management features.

faq.question: What is a commit?
faq.answer: A commit records a project snapshot and metadata in Git history, linked to one or more parent commits.

faq.question: What is a branch?
faq.answer: A branch is a named reference that moves forward as new commits are created, allowing parallel lines of development.
